title: Der Wolf und der Fuchs
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 73. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original scans). 1857 spelling preserved (daß, gieng/giengen, fieng, thun, todt, ward).
about: KHM 73, a beast-fable in three days and one refrain. The fox is the wolf’s unwilling servant, and three times the wolf orders him to fetch food on pain of being eaten himself — a lamb, a dish of pancakes, a cask of salted meat — and three times the wolf’s greed carries him past what the fox provided, into the peasants’ cudgels. Twice the fox answers with the same flat line, “warum bist du so ein Nimmersatt”; on the third day he never has to say it, because the wolf’s appetite settles the matter without him. Spelling follows the 1857 edition, so you will meet gieng, fieng, thun, todt and the ß of mußte.

sentences.t: Der Wolf hatte den Fuchs bei sich, und was der Wolf wollte, das mußte der Fuchs thun, weil er der schwächste war, und der Fuchs wär gerne des Herrn los gewesen.
sentences.l: The wolf had the fox by him, and what the wolf wanted, that the fox had to do, because he was the weakest, and the fox would gladly have been rid of the master.
sentences.i: The wolf kept the fox by him, and whatever the wolf wanted, the fox had to do, because he was the weaker; and the fox would gladly have been rid of his master.
sentences.n: “los sein” = to be rid of something, and here it governs the genitive, des Herrn — rid of the master; modern German uses the accusative, jemanden los sein. It is the wish the whole tale exists to grant. wär is a clipped wäre. der schwächste is a superlative where modern German would rather use the comparative, the weaker of the two.

sentences.t: Es trug sich zu, daß sie beide durch den Wald giengen, da sprach der Wolf „Rothfuchs, schaff mir was zu fressen, oder ich fresse dich selber auf.“
sentences.l: It bore itself to pass that they both went through the forest, then spoke the wolf “Red-fox, get me something to devour, or I devour you yourself up.”
sentences.i: It came to pass that the two of them were going through the forest, and the wolf said: “Red fox, get me something to eat, or I shall eat you instead.”
sentences.n: fressen is the verb for a beast’s eating (essen belongs to people), and everything in this tale eats as a beast. The wolf’s demand returns word for word on each of the three days — the repetition is the tale’s frame.

sentences.t: Da antwortete der Fuchs „ich weiß einen Bauernhof, wo ein paar junge Lämmlein sind, hast du Lust, so wollen wir eins holen.“
sentences.l: Then answered the fox “I know a farmyard where a couple of young little-lambs are, have you a mind, so will we fetch one.”
sentences.i: Then the fox answered: “I know of a farmyard where there are a couple of young lambs; if you have a mind to it, we will fetch one.”
sentences.n: “Lust haben” = to have a mind to something. “hast du Lust, so…” is a condition with no wenn — the verb simply stands first, and so answers it. Lämmlein is the diminutive of Lamm.

sentences.t: Dem Wolf war das recht, sie giengen hin, und der Fuchs stahl das Lämmlein, brachte es dem Wolf und machte sich fort.
sentences.l: To the wolf that was right, they went thither, and the fox stole the little-lamb, brought it to the wolf and made himself off.
sentences.i: That suited the wolf; they went there, and the fox stole the lamb, brought it to the wolf and made himself scarce.
sentences.n: “jemandem ist etwas recht” = it suits someone, with the person in the dative: dem Wolf. “sich fortmachen” = to clear out — the fox leaves before the trouble starts, every time.

sentences.t: Da fraß es der Wolf auf, war aber damit noch nicht zufrieden, sondern wollte das andere dazu haben, und gieng es zu holen.
sentences.l: Then devoured it the wolf up, was however not content with that yet, but rather wanted the other one besides, and went to fetch it.
sentences.i: Then the wolf ate it up, but was not content with that; he wanted the other one too, and went to fetch it.
sentences.n: The pronoun object es runs ahead of the noun subject der Wolf: German puts light pronouns as early in the clause as it can. “gieng es zu holen” builds the purpose on a plain zu-infinitive where modern German would say um es zu holen.

sentences.t: Weil er es aber so ungeschickt machte, ward es die Mutter vom Lämmlein gewahr und fieng an entsetzlich zu schreien und zu bläen, daß die Bauern herbeigelaufen kamen.
sentences.l: Because he however did it so clumsily, became the mother of the little-lamb aware of it and began terribly to cry and to bleat, so that the peasants came running up.
sentences.i: But because he went about it so clumsily, the lamb’s mother became aware of it and began to cry and bleat so horribly that the peasants came running.
sentences.n: “etwas gewahr werden” = to become aware of something; the older construction takes the genitive, and the es here is that genitive. bläen is an older form of blöken (to bleat). ward is the old past of werden (modern wurde).

sentences.t: Da fanden sie den Wolf und schlugen ihn so erbärmlich, daß er hinkend und heulend bei dem Fuchs ankam.
sentences.l: There they found the wolf and beat him so pitifully that he arrived limping and howling at the fox.
sentences.i: There they found the wolf and beat him so dreadfully that he came limping and howling back to the fox.
sentences.n: erbärmlich, “pitiably,” is said here of how hard he was beaten rather than of how he felt. hinkend and heulend are present participles used as adverbs of manner — limping and howling.

sentences.t: „Du hast mich schön angeführt,“ sprach er, „ich wollte das andere Lamm holen, da haben mich die Bauern erwischt und haben mich weich geschlagen.“
sentences.l: “You have led me on finely,” spoke he, “I wanted to fetch the other lamb, then the peasants caught me and have beaten me soft.”
sentences.i: “A fine trick you played on me,” said he. “I meant to fetch the other lamb, and the peasants caught me and beat me soft.”
sentences.n: anführen = to lead by the nose, to dupe; schön is bitter irony. “weich geschlagen” — beaten soft, the word used of pounding meat tender.

sentences.t: Der Fuchs antwortete „warum bist du so ein Nimmersatt.“
sentences.l: The fox answered “why are you such a never-full.”
sentences.i: The fox answered: “Why must you be such a glutton.”
sentences.n: Nimmersatt — “never sated” — is at once a common word for a glutton and this tale’s name for the wolf. The 1857 text ends the line with a full stop, not a question mark: the fox is not really asking, and he will say exactly this again tomorrow.

sentences.t: Am andern Tag giengen sie wieder ins Feld, sprach der gierige Wolf abermals „Rothfuchs, schaff mir was zu fressen, oder ich fresse dich selber auf.“
sentences.l: On the other day they went again into the field, spoke the greedy wolf once more “Red-fox, get me something to devour, or I devour you yourself up.”
sentences.i: The next day they went out into the field again, and the greedy wolf said once more: “Red fox, get me something to eat, or I shall eat you instead.”

sentences.t: Da antwortete der Fuchs „ich weiß ein Bauernhaus, da backt die Frau heut Abend Pfannkuchen, wir wollen uns davon holen.“
sentences.l: Then answered the fox “I know a farmhouse, there bakes the woman this evening pancakes, we will fetch ourselves some of them.”
sentences.i: Then the fox answered: “I know of a farmhouse where the wife is baking pancakes this evening; we will fetch ourselves some.”
sentences.n: da here is the relative “where,” standing in for in dem — a spoken join rather than a formal relative clause. “uns davon holen”: uns is a dative of interest, and davon means some of them.

sentences.t: Sie giengen hin, und der Fuchs schlich ums Haus herum, guckte und schnupperte so lange, bis er ausfindig machte wo die Schüssel stand, zog dann sechs Pfannkuchen herab und brachte sie dem Wolf.
sentences.l: They went thither, and the fox crept around the house, peered and sniffed so long until he found out where the dish stood, then pulled six pancakes down and brought them to the wolf.
sentences.i: They went there, and the fox crept round and round the house, peering and sniffing until he made out where the dish stood; then he pulled six pancakes down and brought them to the wolf.
sentences.n: “um … herum” brackets the phrase at both ends, the herum adding the sense of going all the way round. “ausfindig machen” = to find out; ausfindig exists only inside this phrase.

sentences.t: „Da hast du zu fressen,“ sprach er zu ihm und gieng seiner Wege.
sentences.l: “There you have something to devour,” spoke he to him and went his ways.
sentences.i: “There, that is something to eat,” he said to him, and went his way.
sentences.n: “seiner Wege gehen” = to go one’s way — an old genitive phrase, and plural (Wege) where English keeps the singular.

sentences.t: Der Wolf hatte die Pfannkuchen in einem Augenblick hinunter geschluckt und sprach „sie schmecken nach mehr,“ gieng hin und riß geradezu die ganze Schüssel herunter, daß sie in Stücke zersprang.
sentences.l: The wolf had swallowed the pancakes down in a moment and spoke “they taste of more,” went thither and tore straightway the whole dish down, so that it burst into pieces.
sentences.i: The wolf had gulped the pancakes down in a moment and said, “They taste of more” — then went over and pulled the whole dish straight down, so that it shattered to pieces.
sentences.n: “es schmeckt nach mehr” is a set phrase: it tastes as though more ought to follow, one helping is not enough.

sentences.t: Da gabs einen gewaltigen Lärm, daß die Frau herauskam, und als sie den Wolf sah, rief sie die Leute, die eilten herbei und schlugen ihn was Zeug wollte halten, daß er mit zwei lahmen Beinen laut heulend zum Fuchs in den Wald hinaus kam.
sentences.l: Then there was a mighty noise, so that the woman came out, and when she saw the wolf, she called the people, who hurried up and beat him as much as the stuff would hold, so that he came with two lame legs, loudly howling, out to the fox in the forest.
sentences.i: That raised a mighty din, so that the wife came out; and when she saw the wolf she called the people, who came hurrying and beat him for all they were worth, so that he came out into the forest to the fox with two lame legs, howling aloud.
sentences.n: “schlagen was Zeug wollte halten” — literally “beat as much as the stuff would hold,” that is, as hard as the sticks would stand; a rough country idiom. gabs = gab es.

sentences.t: „Was hast du mich garstig angeführt!“ rief er, „die Bauern haben mich erwischt und mir die Haut gegerbt.“
sentences.l: “How nastily have you led me on!” cried he, “the peasants have caught me and tanned me the hide.”
sentences.i: “What a foul trick you have played on me!” he cried. “The peasants caught me and tanned my hide.”
sentences.n: was here is the exclamatory “how” (modern wie). “die Haut gerben” = to tan someone’s hide, the same picture as in English; mir is the dative of the person it happens to, where English simply says “my hide.”

sentences.t: Der Fuchs aber antwortete „warum bist du so ein Nimmersatt.“
sentences.l: The fox however answered “why are you such a never-full.”
sentences.i: But the fox answered: “Why must you be such a glutton.”

sentences.t: Am dritten Tag, als sie beisammen draußen waren, und der Wolf mit Mühe nur forthinkte, sprach er doch wieder „Rothfuchs, schaff mir was zu fressen, oder ich fresse dich selber auf.“
sentences.l: On the third day, when they were outside together, and the wolf only with effort limped along, spoke he nevertheless again “Red-fox, get me something to devour, or I devour you yourself up.”
sentences.i: On the third day, when they were out together and the wolf could only limp along with difficulty, he said all the same, once again: “Red fox, get me something to eat, or I shall eat you instead.”

sentences.t: Der Fuchs antwortete „ich weiß einen Mann, der hat geschlachtet, und das gesalzene Fleisch liegt in einem Faß im Keller, das wollen wir holen.“
sentences.l: The fox answered “I know a man, he has slaughtered, and the salted meat lies in a cask in the cellar, that we will fetch.”
sentences.i: The fox answered: “I know of a man who has done his slaughtering, and the salted meat lies in a cask in the cellar; that is what we will fetch.”
sentences.n: “der hat geschlachtet” uses der as a plain demonstrative, “he has slaughtered,” rather than as a relative pronoun — a spoken-German join. The autumn slaughtering filled the salt-cask that had to last the winter.

sentences.t: Sprach der Wolf „aber ich will gleich mitgehen, damit du mir hilfst, wenn ich nicht fort kann.“
sentences.l: Spoke the wolf “but I will go along at once, so that you help me if I cannot get away.”
sentences.i: Said the wolf: “But I mean to come along at once, so that you can help me if I cannot get away.”

sentences.t: „Meinetwegen,“ sagte der Fuchs, und zeigte ihm die Schliche und Wege, auf welchen sie endlich in den Keller gelangten.
sentences.l: “For all I care,” said the fox, and showed him the by-paths and ways on which they at last got into the cellar.
sentences.i: “As you please,” said the fox, and showed him the byways and paths by which they at last reached the cellar.
sentences.n: meinetwegen — literally “for my sake” — is the word for grudging consent: as you please, I don’t mind. die Schliche are the secret ways, from schleichen, the verb used of the fox himself earlier.

sentences.t: Da war nun Fleisch im Überfluß, und der Wolf machte sich gleich daran und dachte „bis ich aufhöre, hats Zeit.“
sentences.l: There was now meat in abundance, and the wolf set himself at once to it and thought “until I stop, it has time.”
sentences.i: There was meat in plenty, and the wolf set to at once, thinking, “There is no hurry about my stopping.”
sentences.n: “sich an etwas machen” = to set to work at something. “es hat Zeit” = there is no hurry — so “bis ich aufhöre, hats Zeit” means the question of when he stops can wait.

sentences.t: Der Fuchs ließ sichs auch gut schmecken, blickte überall herum, lief aber oft zu dem Loch, durch welches sie gekommen waren und versuchte ob sein Leib noch schmal genug wäre durchzuschlüpfen.
sentences.l: The fox let it taste good to himself too, looked around everywhere, ran however often to the hole through which they had come and tried whether his body were still slender enough to slip through.
sentences.i: The fox too made a good meal of it, and looked about him everywhere, but he ran often to the hole they had come through and tried whether his body were still slender enough to slip out.
sentences.n: “sich etwas gut schmecken lassen” = to eat with relish, literally to let something taste good to oneself. wäre is subjunctive after ob, holding the outcome open. The fox eats and measures himself; the wolf only eats.

sentences.t: Sprach der Wolf „lieber Fuchs, sag mir warum rennst du so hin und her, und springst hinaus und herein?“
sentences.l: Spoke the wolf “dear fox, tell me why do you run so to and fro, and spring out and in?”
sentences.i: Said the wolf: “Dear fox, tell me, why do you run to and fro like this, and spring out and in?”
sentences.n: hin and her are the two halves of German’s direction system: hin points away from where the speaker is, her toward it. So hin und her is to and fro, hinaus is out and herein is in; the same pair builds hinab, herauf and the rest.

sentences.t: „Ich muß doch sehen, ob niemand kommt,“ antwortete der listige, „friß nur nicht zu viel.“
sentences.l: “I must after all see whether nobody comes,” answered the cunning one, “only don’t devour too much.”
sentences.i: “I must see that no one is coming,” answered the sly one. “Only don’t eat too much.”
sentences.n: “der listige” is an adjective standing alone as a noun, the cunning one; the 1857 text leaves it lowercase. His advice is the one honest thing he says, and the wolf ignores it.

sentences.t: Da sagte der Wolf „ich gehe nicht eher fort, als bis das Faß leer ist.“
sentences.l: Then said the wolf “I go not away sooner than until the cask is empty.”
sentences.i: Then the wolf said: “I shall not go until the cask is empty.”
sentences.n: “nicht eher… als bis” = not until, no sooner than — a heavy old way of putting it.

sentences.t: Indem kam der Bauer, der den Lärm von des Fuchses Sprüngen gehört hatte, in den Keller.
sentences.l: In that moment came the peasant, who had heard the noise of the fox’s leaps, into the cellar.
sentences.i: Just then the peasant, who had heard the noise of the fox’s leaping, came into the cellar.
sentences.n: indem is used here as an adverb of time, “just then” — the older sense; in modern German indem is a conjunction meaning “by doing.” “des Fuchses Sprüngen” sets the genitive in front of its noun, an elevated older order.

sentences.t: Der Fuchs, wie er ihn sah, war mit einem Satz zum Loch draußen: der Wolf wollte nach, aber er hatte sich so dick gefressen, daß er nicht mehr durch konnte, sondern stecken blieb.
sentences.l: The fox, as he saw him, was with one bound out at the hole: the wolf wanted after, but he had eaten himself so fat that he could no longer through, but rather stuck fast.
sentences.i: The fox, the moment he saw him, was out at the hole in a single bound; the wolf tried to follow, but he had eaten himself so fat that he could get through no longer, and stuck fast.
sentences.n: Satz here is a bound or a leap, not a sentence. “wollte nach” and “konnte durch” leave the verb of motion unsaid — German lets a modal plus a direction stand on its own. “sich dick fressen” = to eat oneself fat.

sentences.t: Da kam der Bauer mit einem Knüppel und schlug ihn todt.
sentences.l: Then came the peasant with a cudgel and struck him dead.
sentences.n: todt is the 1857 spelling of tot, and “todt schlagen” — to strike dead — is one of German’s free verb-plus-result pairs. der Knüppel is the thick stick a peasant has to hand.

sentences.t: Der Fuchs aber sprang in den Wald und war froh daß er den alten Nimmersatt los war.
sentences.l: The fox however sprang into the forest and was glad that he was rid of the old never-full.
sentences.i: But the fox sprang off into the forest, glad to be rid of the old glutton at last.
sentences.n: The tale closes on the wish it opened with — the fox “wär gerne des Herrn los gewesen” — granted in the end by the wolf’s own appetite rather than by any trick of his.
